title: Machine learning prediction of CKD progression in hyperglycemic elderly adults: a prospective community cohort study

paragraphs.en: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a pressing global health crisis, impacting approximately 10% of the population worldwide [1]. By 2021, over 670 million people worldwide lived with CKD [2]. Projections to become the fifth leading cause of death by 2040, it underscores an urgent need for enhanced preventive strategies [3]. Hyperglycemia, spanning both prediabetes and diabetes, significantly elevates CKD risk through mechanisms like advanced glycation end-product accumulation, glomerular hyperfiltration, and microvascular damage [4]. Prediabetes is increasingly recognized as a substantial risk factor for CKD onset [5,6], while an estimated 40%–50% of individuals with diabetes will develop CKD [7,8]. Early screening for CKD risk in individuals with hyperglycemia is therefore critical for effective prevention and management.

Older adults are at high risk of diabetic nephropathy (DN)[9]. Global data indicate that most DN-related deaths occur in individuals over 55 years and the highest rates in those over 70 years [10]. The dual burden of increasing obesity prevalence and population aging is expected to further expand the population of older adults with diabetes progressing to CKD [11]. China, home to the world’s largest diabetic population, has an estimated 39 million community-dwelling older adults with concurrent diabetes and CKD [12]. Early intervention for kidney disease yields far better outcomes than late-stage treatment, developing predictive models to identify early CKD risk in individuals with impaired glucose metabolism is essential [13].

Although multiple CKD prediction models exist for hyperglycemic individuals, most lack external validation, community application evidence and inclusion of prediabetic patients [14–18]. Machine learning (ML), a branch of artificial intelligence (AI), performs better than traditional statistical methods in predictive accuracy and enables scalable risk stratification using routine electronic health records (EHR) [19–20]. The American Society of Nephrology further points out that AI is widely applied in EHR documentation generation, and innovative AI based tools can provide actionable guidance for individual patients and nephrology specialists [21]. This prospective study aims to develop and externally validate an interpretable ML based CKD prediction model for community dwelling elderly hyperglycemic patients, covering both diabetic and prediabetic individuals. Ultimately, we aim to build a model that acts as a learning health system node to support better CKD management.

This multicenter prospective cohort study adhered to TRIPOD-AI (Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis, Extended for Artificial Intelligence) and PROBAST-AI (Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool, Extended for Artificial Intelligence) guidelines to ensure transparent model development, validation, and bias assessment [22,23]. Completed TRIPOD-AI and PROBAST-AI checklists are provided in Appendix 1 and Appendix 2. The Medical Ethics Committee of Tongji University School of Medicine granted approval for this study (Ethics No. 2020tjdx068).

We enrolled community-dwelling adults aged ≥60 years with hyperglycemia (including prediabetes and diabetes) from four Shanghai communities (Anting, Gonghexin Road, Huamu Road, and Nanxiang), all wih ≥ year annual follow-up. Study periods and sample sizes were as follows: Anting (2021–2024, n = 5862), Gonghexin Road (2016–2019, n = 3174), Huamu Road (2016–2018, n = 1981), and Nanxiang (2018–2021, n = 4561). Baseline data from Anting, Gonghexin Road, and Huamu Road were pooled and randomly split into training (80%, n = 8814) and internal test (20%, n = 2203) sets. Participants from Nanxiang served as the validation set. Participants were excluded in they had: (1) less than two follow-up visits; (2) age < 60 years; (3) normal glucose metabolism; (4) preexisting CKD; and (5) malignant tumors (Figure 1).

Sample size was calculated using esablished methods [24,25] based on the ‘events per variable’ (EPV) principle, requiring ≥10–15 outcome events per predictor while accounting for overall event rate and total sample size. For our 10-predictor model, the minimum required events were derived from n ≥ k × 15 (k = number of predictors), necessitating at least 150 events. Using the observed event rate (p ≈ 9.48%, 836/8815) and the formula n ≥ [(k × 10)/p], we estimated a minimum total of 1572 participants. The training set (n = 8815, 836 events) substantially exceeded these thresholds, confirming adequacy. Both external (n = 4561, 492 events) and internal (n = 2202, 208 events) validation sets also satisfied the requirements.

CKD was defined by any of the following: (1) at least one occurrence of ≥40% eGFR decline; (2) at least two self-reported diagnoses of CKD; (3) at least two measurements of eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m2. Participants with only one positive test result or self-reported event were excluded.

The 2009 Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI 2009) formula was used to calculate eGFR [26]. Self-reported CKD was ascertained by physicians during physical examinations through inquiries about past medical or hospitalization history, including conditions such as glomerulonephritis, nephrotic syndrome, diabetic nephropathy, hypertensive nephropathy, and obstructive nephropathy.

Hyperglycemia was defined as meeting any of the following criteria [27,28]: (1) Prediabetes: Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) 5.7%–6.5% or fasting plasma glucose (FPG) 5.6–7.0 mmol/L; (2) Diabetes: HbA1c ≥ 6.5% or FPG ≥ 7.0 mmol/L; (3) Self-reported diabetes or current use of antidiabetic medications.

Covariates were collected via questionnaires and clinical assessments. Sociodemographic data (sex, age), lifestyle factors (smoking, drinking, exercise), self-reported diseases, and hospitalization history were captured via questionnaires. Smoking and drinking statuses were categorized as ‘yes’ or ‘no’ based on current engagement in these behaviors. Physical activity was stratified into three levels by weekly duration: level 1 (<150 min); level 2 (150–300 min); level 3 (≥300 min) [29].

Clinical assessments included anthropometric measurements of height, weight, waist circumference (WC), hip circumference (HC), pulse, systolic blood pressure (SBP), and diastolic blood pressure (DBP). Laboratory tests were performed on fasting venous blood and urine samples, with the following indicators assessed: red blood cells (RBC), white blood cells (WBC), platelets (PLT), hemoglobin (Hb), total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), FPG, HbA1c, total bilirubin (TBIl), uric acid (UA), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and serum creatinine (Scr). All tests were performed at the central hospital laboratory of each community using standardized protocols.

Feature selection was performed in the training set. Variables with a missing rate < 15% were imputed via multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) [30], and continuous variables were standardized. To avoid data leakage, missing data in the training and validation sets were imputed separately; details of missing data are shown in Figure S1. Feature selection was carried out via the Boruta algorithm and Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression. The Boruta algorithm ranks features based on random forests, while LASSO regression employs L1 norm regularization [31,32]. Multicollinearity was assessed to examine variable correlations; for variables with a Spearman correlation coefficient >0.6, the one with greater clinical relevance was retained to eliminate collinearity.

Five machine learning (ML) models were developed using training set: logistic regression (LR), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), random forest (RF), light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM), and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost). Each model underwent hyperparameter optimization and 5-fold cross-validation to ensure reliability and we employed grid search for hyperparameter tuning. Model evaluation covers three aspects: discriminative power, calibration, and clinical utility. Discriminative power is evaluated by drawing receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, with calculation of the area under the curve (AUC) and its 95% confidence intervals (95% CI); DeLong tests were used to compare AUCs between models. Calibration was measured via calibration curves, with the Brier score and Hosmer-Lemeshow tests quantifying the agreement between predicted probabilities and observed outcomes. Clinical utility was determined using decision curve analysis (DCA), which estimates net benefit across different risk thresholds. Additional performance metrics included accuracy, specificity, sensitivity, precision, recall, F1-score, and geometric mean accuracy (G-mean). The cutoff value was defined as the probability corresponding to the maximum Youden index (sensitivity + specificity − 1). To stratify predicted risks into low, medium and high categories, the Log-Rank test was adopted to identify optimal stratification thresholds. Specifically, we conducted multi-node candidate partitioning on continuous predicted risk values, traversed different threshold combinations repeatedly, calculated the Log-Rank test P-values of survival curves among different risk groups for each candidate threshold, and finally selected the two nodes with the smallest P-values. These nodes indicate the most obvious differences in the incidence of CKD progression events between groups. The newly developed models were compared with the Chien equation, a validated tool that dose not require urine test data [33]. Developed by Chien et al. using 5,168 Chinese participants (Taiwan, China), this equation predicts CKD using age, BMI, diastolic blood pressure, and histories of diabetes and stroke [34].

Model interpretability was enhanced using the Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) method [35]. This approach quantifies SHAP values to decompose ML model outputs, enabling assessment of feature importance at both global and local levels, as well as characterization of feature dependencies and variable interactions. Additionally, SHAP facilitates visualization of feature impacts on individual sample predictions.

To enhance clinical applicability, we stratified the study population by predicted CKD risk and developed an online application as a node of the learning health system to enable rapid, user-friendly risk assessment.

Sensitivity analyses were performed to evaluate the robustness of study findings using three approaches. First, we applied stricter baseline CKD exclusion criteria, including only participants with no CKD diagnosis in two consecutive years. Second, to address potential data imbalance (a known confounder of ML model performance), we applied the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) to the training set [36]. Third, we conducted subgroup analyses to explore whether population heterogeneity influenced model performance.

Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation, and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Normally distributed continuous variables were compared between groups using the two-sample t-test, while non-normally distributed continuous variables were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test. All statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.4.2) with the following packages: ‘caret,’ ‘glmnet,’ ‘xgboost,’ ‘class,’ ‘lightgbm,’ ‘randomForest,’ ‘shapviz’, ‘shiny’, and others. A two-sided p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

During follow-up, the incidence of CKD was 9.48% (836/8815) in the training set, 9.45% (208/2202) in the internal validation set, and 10.79% (492/4561) in the external validation set (Table S1). Feature selection procedures are presented in Figure 2 and Figures S2, S3. From an initial 31 variables, 10 were provisionally selected as the intersection of Boruta and LASSO regression: Scr, Age, SBP, HbA1c, Hb, TG, HDL-C, UA, BMI, BUN.

Models were developed using the training set, with baseline characteristics summarized in Table 1. All 10 variables included in the models differed significantly between partipipants with and withoud CKD (all p < 0.001): partipipants with CKD were older and had higher levels of Scr, SBP, HbA1c, TG, UA, BUN, and BMI, but lower levels of Hb and HDL-C levels.

sections.title: Comparison and evaluation of ML models

paragraphs.en: Figure 3 and Figures S4, S5 presented a detailed comparison and evaluation of the five ML models. Both the RF model and XGBoost model performed well on the training set, with AUC values exceeding 0.9. However, XGBoost demonstrated superior stability: its AUC was 0.905 (95%CI 0.894–0.915) in the training set, 0.809 (95% CI 0.779–0.839) in the test set, and 0.837 (95% CI 0.818–0.856) in the external validation set. Furthermore, in the training set, XGBoost’s AUC significantly higher than that of all other models (all DeLong tests, p < 0.05) (Table S2).

The XGBoost model showed optimal calibration: it had the lowest Brier score (0.058) in the training set, and good scores in the test (0.073) and validation (0.077) sets. The Hosmer-Lemeshow test (p > 0.05 for internal set) confirmed no gap between predicted and true probabilities, while slope/intercept values and the largest R2 further supported its ideal calibration.

DCA results confirmed that XGBoost achieved a robust net benefit and clinically meaningful efficacy. Considering discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility, the XGBoost model was identified as the optimal model. Its detailed performance metrics are presented in Table 2: accuracy = 0.782, specificity = 0.773, sensitivity = 0.866, precision = 0.286, recall = 0.866, F1-score = 0.430, and G-mean = 0.818.

The optimal XGBoost model was selected to dissect its predictive logic. Key parameters were: learning_rate = 0.07, max_depth = 3, nrounds = 285, early_stop_round = 5, gamma = 0.5, subsample = 0.9, colsample_bytree = 0.8, min_child_weight = 3, and eval_metric = ‘auc’. Model-derived feature importance identified Scr, SBP, age, Hb, and UA as the top five contributors (Figure S6). SHAP values were used to elucidate the model’s inner logic, where higher SHAP values indicate stronger predictive contributions to CKD. The top three features are Scr, Age, and Hb, accounting for 24.5%, 18.8%, and 14.7% of total predictive power, respectively (Figure 4A,B). A SHAP honeycomb plot (Figure 4C) revealed positive correlations between Scr/age and SHAP values, and a negative correlation between Hb and SHAP vaules.

Figure S7 was generated using representative samples to visualize the contribution of each feature’s SHAP value to the model output: blue denotes negative contributions (reducing risk), and red denotes positive contributions (increasing risk). The combined effects of these feature-specific contributions determined the final prediction probability. Loess regression curves were fitted to scatter plots of SHAP values for the top three features, crossing the SHAP = 0 line at Scr 73.19 μmol/L, age 71.24 years, and Hb 137.61 g/L (Figure S8).

Using predicted probability density distribution and log-rank test results, we set 5% and 25% as risk stratification cutoffs, defining three risk tiers: low (0%–5%), medium (5%–25%), and high (25%–100%). Corresponding actual CKD incidence rates were 0.7%, 9.9%, and 55.5%. For comparison, the Chien equation yielded incidence rates of 3.7%, 9.8%, and 20.5% across the same tiers, demonstrating our model’s superior ability to identify high-risk populations (Figure 5A,B). Given the >50% actual CKD incidence in the high-risk tier, a predicted probability >25% was defined as a positive CKD prediction. Similar to the principle of a waterfall plot, force plots were used to visualize individual feature contributions to a single-sample prediction. To enhance clinical applicability, we developed an online application using R’s Shiny package. An example of a webpage is shown in Figure 5C. Users can input variables such as Scr and age to generate a preliminary CKD risk prediction. A user manual is provided in Appendix 3 and the application is accessible at: https://zhouzhongqing.shinyapps.io/CKDPredictor/.

With fixed XGBoost parameters, sensitivity analyses (Tables S3–S4) confirmed the modelʼs robust performance (all AUC > 0.9). These results indicated that SMOTE, stricter baseline CKD exclusion creteria, and population subgroup differences had no significant impact on model performance.

Using multicenter prospective cohort data, we developed and validated a ML model to predict CKD risk in community-dwelling older adults with hyperglycemia. The XGBoost model demonstrated optimal performance, highlighting its potential for clinical translation in this high-risk population. Key findings highlighted Scr, age, and Hb as primary predictors: elevated Scr, advanced age, and reduced Hb were associated with increased predicted CKD risk. Notably, the high-risk subgroup (prediction probability >25%) exhibited an observed CKD incidence exceeding 50%, emphasizing the urgent need for targeted early interventions in this vulnerable cohort.

Existing literature on CKD prediction in glucose metabolism-impaired populations has focused largely on diabetic individuals, overlooking prediabetic groups [14–17,37,38]. For instance, Dunkler et al. developed a logistic regression model in 6,766 diabetic patients aged 55 years or older, identifying eGFR as the primary predictor of early CKD (C-statistic = 0.69) [37]. Tangri et al. validated the Klinrisk ML model in type 2 diabetes, reporting AUCs of 0.81 (95% CI 0.78–0.83) at 1 year and 0.88 (95% CI 0.86–0.89) at 3 years [38]. By including both diabetic and prediabetic individuals, this study comprehensively covers the glucose metabolism impairment spectrum, critical, as prediabetes is not merely a transitional state but an independent risk factor for adverse outcomes [39]. Moreover, integrating multidimensional features via machine learning enhanced model performance.

The performance of ML algorithms depends on data quality, and in cohort studies, follow-up duration is a key determinant [40]. Community-dwelling older adults aged 60+ often exhibit multiple chronic conditions and rapid changes in physical function [41]. Shorter follow-up periods help capture these dynamics promptly, minimizing data loss from participant disability or mortality. Since this study aims to identify high-risk populations early via predictive models, shorter follow-up aligns with the ‘early detection and intervention’ needs of community chronic disease management [42]. Moreover, community medical practice demands a balance between timeliness and practicality: shorter follow-up data reflects recent disease risk profiles and avoids key factors change from prolonged follow-up, such as shifts in population structure, updated clinical guidelines, or staff changes [43]. This study included community-dwelling older adults, with a 2–3-year follow-up period intentionally chosen to balance timeliness and event capture for early detection.

Feature selection, a pivotal preprocessing step to enhance data quality, was conducted prior to model development to identify the most informative subset of variables from the initial dataset [44]. As datasets grow in size and complexity, the number of features often increases significantly, but some may be redundant or introduce noise [45]. By reducing dimensionality, feature selection improves training efficiency, simplifies model architecture for enhanced interpretability, focuses on core information to strengthen generalizability, and mitigates overfitting risks [46]. This study employed LASSO regression and the Boruta algorithm [31,32]. After taking the intersection of their results, collinearity analysis and clinical expertise were combined to finally select 10 features for modeling, reducing interference from irrelevant information.

ML models exhibit distinct characteristics [47]. Logistic regression, with low computational complexity, enables rapid processing of large datasets and outputs interpretable coefficients that clarify feature influence direction and magnitude. However, it only captures linear relationships, limiting its utility to linearly separable binary classification tasks and risking underfitting with complex or non-linearly separable data [48]. Random forests handle non-linear interactions and noise robustly but lack interpretability and may overfit noisy data [49]. XGBoost, using gradient boosting with regularization, achieves high predictive accuracy by balancing non-linear relationship capture, generalizability, and efficiency, while providing feature importance metrics [50,51].

Model performance varied by algorithm, necessitating cross-validation to optimize test set outcomes. Model quality was evaluated across three dimensions: discriminative power, calibration, and clinical utility [52]. Discriminative power, while fundamental for identifying risk group differences, is insufficient alone due to clinical complexity [53]. For example, management strategies differ for 45% vs. 90% predicted risk. Calibration ensures predicted risks reflect true outcomes, and clinical utility guides tradeoffs between false positives/negatives based on disease-specific needs [54]. Considering all aspects, the XGBoost model demonstrated superior performance across all three metrics, outperforming the Chien equation [34] in predictive accuracy. Its external validation AUC of 0.815 exceeded the C-statistics (0.69–0.81) of previous diabetes-specific models [55], confirming robust generalizability.

Model development aligned with guidelines like the FDAʼs Predictive Computational Drug Safety (PCDS) framework, emphasizing population-specific validation and transparent decision-making [56]. Our model meets these requirements: it was validated in 4 independent communities of hyperglycemic community-dwelling older adults, and SHAP analysis provided the FDA-required ‘meaningful explanation’ to avoid opaque ‘black-box’ outputs. SHAP helps clarify key outcome predictors and their directional impacts [57,58]. We identified Scr, age, and Hb as the top three predictors. Specifically, elevated Scr, advanced age, and reduced Hb levels were linked to higher CKD onset risk. These findings align with established renal physiological mechanisms [59,60], demonstrating how interpretable ML bridges algorithmic outputs with clinical knowledge. This case study highlights the value of interpretable ML in connecting predictive models to real-world medical understanding, offering a reference for developing transparent tools for other chronic diseases.

To enhance clinical utility, the prediction model was deployed as an online Shiny-based learning health system node, enabling early CKD screening in community-dwelling older adults. By translating individualized risk into actionable steps, this tool supports stratified management: high-risk patients can be prioritized for nephrology referral and early intervention [61], while those at moderate risk may benefit from intensified control of modifiable factors [62]. Such risk-aligned care pathways position the application as a promising adjunct to routine CKD practice.

The application holds particular relevance for diabetes screening workflows. Endocrinologists typically lead CKD screening for patients with or at risk of diabetes [63], i making this tool directly applicable during routine diabetes assessments. For instance, when impaired glucose tolerance is detected or a new diabetes diagnosis is established, clinicians can simultaneously evaluate concurrent CKD risk using the application. This integrated approach aligns with clinical guidelines advocating parallel evaluation of diabetes and kidney health, enabling proactive rather than sequential management of both conditions. By streamlining dual risk assessment, the tool may mitigate fragmented care and enhance comprehensive management of patients with overlapping metabolic and renal risk factors.

The application’s user-friendly online format and simplicity make it ideal for population-wide CKD screening, particularly targeting high-risk groups such as community-dwelling older adults and individuals with hyperglycemia. From a cost-effectiveness perspective, the tool can efficiently identify low-risk individuals, thereby reducing unnecessary advanced diagnostics, such as repeated renal function panels or imaging, in this group. Concurrently, early intervention for high-risk patients may prevent progression to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). ESKD is linked to substantial long-term healthcare costs, including those for dialysis, transplantation, and management of cardiovascular comorbidities [64].

This study has three main strengths. First, it makes use of accessible health data infrastructure. Routine free health checkups for the elderly in Chinese cities, combined with well-established community-based systems [65,66], have enabled efficient collection of high quality data on community dwelling older adults. This decentralized practice-based data collection framework not only supports longitudinal chronic disease research in this population, but also makes the model a potential candidate for federated learning across Chinese community health systems. Second, objective indicators such as FBG, HbA1c, and eGFR were prioritized for clinical outcome assessment, minimizing recall bias associated with self-reported data. This approach enhances data accuracy, reliability, and the robustness of research conclusions [67]. Third, SHAP analysis clarified individual CKD risk drivers (e.g., elevated serum creatinine, higher glycated hemoglobin), supporting personalized patient consultations and enabling clinicians to tailor preventive strategies.

This study has several limitations. First, the absence of urine test data precluded calculation of the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR). Althouth CKD was diagnosed using criteria (eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 in at least two measurements), incorporating multi-dimensional data like UACR could further enhance model performance. Second, we limited model development to five common ML algorithms, potentially restricting the exploration of more diverse ML approaches. Third, this study data were sourced solely from Shanghai communities, limiting the model’s generalizability. Regional variations in ethnicity, lifestyle, and healthcare systems may further impact its transferability to other populations, and these factors require careful consideration when promoting the model.

Future research will address current limitations by focusing on three key priorities to enhance the generalizability, clinical relevance, and methodological rigor of the ML-based CKD risk prediction model for hyperglycemic older adults. First, large-scale multicenter and multinational cohorts encompassing diverse racial, socioeconomic, and healthcare backgrounds will be used for external validation and model recalibration, extending applicability beyond the current urban population. Second, the model was optimized to improve predictive accuracy by incorporating additional predictors such as UACR, inflammatory markers and wearable proxy indicators (e.g., anemia-related fatigue signals). Third, prospective implementation studies and pragmatic clinical trials will assess whether model-guided risk stratification and the use of the online application improve clinical decision-making, facilitate earlier nephrology referral, slow CKD progression, and enhance cost-effectiveness in real-world community settings. Finally, adaptive techniques such as federated learning, transfer learning, and continuous model updating will be explored to maintain long-term performance, protect data privacy, and support sustainable deployment of interpretable AI tools for population-level chronic disease management.

We developed an interpretable ML model using the XGBoost algorithm, demonstrating robust predictive performance in internal and external validation. Packaged as an online application as a node of the learning health system, the tool enables efficient risk stratification, particularly critical for the high-risk subgroup (observed CKD incidence exceeds 50%), who require prioritized clinical intervention. Future research should incorporate more diverse, multi-dimensional datasets to strengthen the model’s representativeness and broader applicability.

figures.caption: The logic of data cleansing and analysis.

figures.label: Figure 2.
figures.caption: Boruta algorithm for variable selection in training data. (A) Feature importance ranking via the Boruta algorithm: The horizontal axis shows variable names, and the vertical axis represents Z-values for each variable. Box plots display Z-values calculated during modeling, with green boxes indicating important variables and red boxes indicating unimportant ones. (B) The iterative process of the Boruta algorithm.

figures.label: Figure 3.
figures.caption: Model evaluation in training set. (A) Calibration curves. The X-axis is the predicted probability, and the Y-axis is the actual occurrence probability, which are used to evaluate the model’s accuracy in predicting probabilities. (B) ROC curves. The X-axis represents the false positive rate (1 - specificity), and the Y-axis represents the true positive rate (sensitivity), which are used to evaluate the model’s discriminatory power. (C) Decision curves. The X-axis is the threshold probability, and the Y-axis is the net benefit, which are used to evaluate the model’s value in clinical decision-making.

figures.label: Figure 4.
figures.caption: SHAP analysis. (A) Feature importance based on SHAP values. (B) Weight of feature importance. (C) Overview of SHAP Value Distribution: The X-axis represents SHAP values (quantifying the degree of feature influence on prediction results), and the Y-axis lists feature names. The distribution pattern (kurtosis and dispersion) illustrates the positive/negative direction and strength of SHAP values for different features.

figures.label: Figure 5.
figures.caption: Risk stratification and web application. (A) CKD Predicted Probability Density Distribution: This chart presents the density distribution patterns of predicted probabilities across two groups (Normal and CKD). It uses curves and statistical data to compare differences in the distribution of predicted probabilities between the two populations. (B) CKD Incidence Rate by Risk Group Proportion: A stacked bar chart shows the proportion of Normal and CKD populations within the Low, Medium, and High risk groups, visually illustrating the association between risk stratification and CKD incidence. (C) CKD Prediction application for Community-Dwelling Elderly with Hyperglycemia: This section showcases a CKD risk prediction tool developed using the XGBoost model. It includes input indicators (e.g., age, systolic blood pressure), prediction outputs (risk level, probability), and SHAP-based visualization of feature contributions, designed for practical risk assessment scenarios.
